arguments.issue: Did the trial judge confuse the insanity defence under s. 16 Cr. C. with the defence of self-induced intoxication under s. 33.1 Cr. C.?
arguments.claim: The trial judge confused the insanity defence with self-induced intoxication defence, leading to misapplication of s. 33.1 Cr. C.
arguments.quote: In general terms, the appellant argued that the trial judge had confused the insanity defence under s. 16 Cr. C. with the defence of self‑induced intoxication under s. 33.1 Cr. C.
arguments.weak_spot: The Court of Appeal held s. 33.1 Cr. C. applies to prevent intoxicated individuals from avoiding liability.

arguments.issue: Is toxic psychosis caused by a single episode of intoxication a "mental disorder" under s. 16 Cr. C.?
arguments.claim: A single episode of intoxication causing toxic psychosis should be considered a mental disorder under s. 16 Cr. C.
arguments.quote: According to him, any toxic psychosis, even one that results, as the trial judge found in this case, from a single episode of intoxication, must be considered a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C.
arguments.weak_spot: The courts found toxic psychosis resulted exclusively from self-induced intoxication, not a pre-existing mental disorder.

arguments.issue: Does s. 33.1 Cr. C. limit the scope of the defence of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder?
arguments.claim: Section 33.1 Cr. C. should not limit the defence of mental disorder; it was intended to exclude self-induced intoxication as a defence for general intent offences.
arguments.quote: Parliament, in enacting s. 33.1 Cr. C., endorsed the position taken by the dissenting judges in Daviault that, owing to policy considerations, the defence of self‑induced intoxication should not be available in the case of a general intent offence.
arguments.weak_spot: The majority in Daviault and the Court of Appeal interpret s. 33.1 Cr. C. as limiting the mental disorder defence when intoxication is self-induced.
